_comment: Hand-maintained per-day notes. Not generated - build_data.py never touches this file, so edits here survive a rebuild. 'watch' items are things to plan around; 'highlights' are things worth looking up for; 'region' describes the farming and wine country the day crosses. Figures quoted in highlights and watch come from data/day-N.json or data/shade.json, so re-check them if a route changes. The 'region' lines are background rather than measurement: the AVA names and the towns are checked against the route, the crops are general knowledge.

highlights: Leaves Los Altos through the Santa Cruz Mountains — the redwood miles are the shadiest of the whole trip at 18%.
Descends to the coast at Santa Cruz; Capitola is a short detour off the end.
watch: The one sustained climb is mi 22.5–24.8, 639 ft at 5.3%. It comes when legs are fresh but it is the day's crux.
1.region: Starts across the Santa Clara Valley, orchard country until the 1960s and built over since, then climbs into the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA — one of California's oldest, and among its coolest and steepest, worked by small producers scattered through the redwoods rather than in open blocks of vineyard.

highlights: Flat coastal day along Monterey Bay, the gentlest climbing of the trip at 1,640 ft.
Moss Landing sits right on the route at roughly halfway — a good lunch stop.
watch: Nothing steeper than 3.5% anywhere on the route — the least climbing of the whole trip at 1,640 ft.
2.region: The Pajaro Valley behind Watsonville is one of the largest strawberry and cane-berry districts in the country; the low ground either side of the road is berries under plastic for much of the year. Nearer the coast it turns to artichokes and brussels sprouts, and at Moss Landing the route passes Elkhorn Slough, a tidal estuary and one of the better bird sites on this coast.

highlights: Carmel Valley Road is a well-known cycling route — the run out of Monterey and Carmel to Carmel Valley Village is ridden constantly by local clubs.
Carmel Valley Village is on the route early; Carmel-by-the-Sea is 0.6 mi off.
The shadiest of the inland days at 24% tree cover — three times the alternate route.
watch: You ride well past the popular section. Beyond Carmel Valley Village the road narrows — OpenStreetMap has it dropping from four lanes to one — and empties out through Jamesburg.
Longest day so far at 70.5 mi with 3,987 ft. The long grind is mi 30.5–34.3, 825 ft at 4.1%, out in the remote eastern stretch.
Only two mapped water points, and a 57 mi stretch without one. Carry for the whole day.
3.region: Begins in the Carmel Valley AVA, a warm pocket that sits behind the coastal fog, then crosses the Santa Lucias and drops into the Salinas Valley at Greenfield around mile 56. This is the ground that gets called America's Salad Bowl — lettuce, broccoli, spinach and celery, a large share of the national crop, grown in long flat blocks between the two ranges. The bench above Greenfield and Soledad is the Santa Lucia Highlands AVA, planted mostly to pinot noir and chardonnay.

highlights: Remote oak country through Jolon and the Nacimiento backcountry, with no highway miles at all.
Lake Nacimiento appears on the descent toward Paso Robles.
watch: The hardest day: 62.6 mi, 4,005 ft, and only 4% shade. Start as early as you can.
No mapped water anywhere on the route, and effectively nothing between mile 1 and mile 48. This is the day the SAG car matters most.
Steepest sustained pitch of the trip at mi 42.2–43.8, 639 ft at 7.5% — and it comes late.
4.region: Leaves the irrigated valley floor almost immediately. Most of the day is oak savanna and cattle ranching through Jolon and the Fort Hunter Liggett country — dry-farmed and thinly settled, which is why there is so little on the route. Vineyards reappear on the approach to Paso Robles.

highlights: Crosses the coast range on Highway 41 and drops to Morro Bay, then runs south past Los Osos.
Templeton and Los Osos are both on the route; Morro Rock is the landmark at the coast.
watch: The Highway 41 climb is mi 17.6–19.0, 388 ft at 5.4% — steady rather than steep.
Highway 41 over the grade is a main road between US-101 and Highway 1, so expect through traffic. Nobody has checked the shoulder — worth asking someone who has ridden it.
5.region: Starts in the Paso Robles AVA, one of California's largest, where hot days and cool nights suit cabernet and the rhône varieties; the vineyards run right up to the edge of town. Crossing the range on Highway 41 the planting stops abruptly, and the coastal side is vegetable ground and pasture around Los Osos and Oceano.

highlights: The best day for small towns: Arroyo Grande Village, Nipomo, Sisquoc, Los Olivos and Ballard are all on or near the route.
Rides the length of Foxen Canyon through the Santa Maria Valley wine country — tasting rooms are the main thing open along the middle of the day.
watch: No mapped tree cover anywhere on the route — 0%, the only day on the trip with none.

The longest stretch without anywhere to stop is 17 mi, from Santa Maria to the Riverbench winery. Between there and Los Olivos the stops are tasting rooms, whose hours are far less dependable than a shop.
Late climb at mi 43.5–44.4, 301 ft at 6.6%, when the day is nearly done.
6.region: The wine day. Santa Maria around mile 18 sits in one of the state's biggest strawberry and broccoli districts, then Foxen Canyon is the spine of the Santa Maria Valley AVA — a cool, wind-exposed valley that opens west to the ocean, which is why pinot noir and chardonnay do well this far south. The last stretch into Los Olivos and Solvang crosses into the Santa Ynez Valley AVA.

highlights: The coastal miles are the prettiest of the trip: Gaviota, Refugio, El Capitán, then Santa Barbara and Carpinteria.
Best-served day by far — 35 water points and the shortest dry stretch at 19 mi.
watch: Longest day of the trip at 82.4 mi, but the climbing is front-loaded: the hardest pitch is mi 4.4–5.2 at 5.9%, and it eases after.
Sections through the Gaviota corridor are ridden on the US-101 freeway shoulder. It is a wide shoulder — noisy and fast alongside, but there is room.
7.region: Leaves the Santa Ynez Valley and runs the Gaviota coast, which is cattle ranchland and largely undeveloped — a rare stretch of open California coastline. From Goleta onward it turns to lemon and avocado groves on the slopes above the road, and Carpinteria is cut flowers and nursery glass, an industry that has been there for a century.

highlights: Final day down the coast through Ventura and Malibu into Santa Monica.
One of the two easiest days for climbing, at 1,661 ft.
watch: Pacific Coast Highway traffic is heavy and fast, especially through Malibu on a Saturday. Be prepared to ride two-by-two, take the lane, and stay together.
Only real climb is mi 38.6–39.3, 185 ft at 5.1%.
8.region: The first hour crosses the Oxnard Plain, among the most productive vegetable and strawberry ground in the United States and still farmed hard right up to the edge of the city. After Point Mugu the farming stops and the rest of the day is the Malibu coast.
